The Bobo Doll Experiment. In 1961, Albert Bandura, Dorothy Ross, and Sheila Ross conducted experiments that challenged one of the core assumptions of Skinnerian psychology. They showed that children could learn behaviour through observation and modelling alone, without direct reinforcement.

The experiment was straightforward. Children aged three to six watched either a live adult or a filmed adult beating an inflatable Bobo doll—kicking, punching, and hitting it while saying aggressive things. A control group saw no aggression. Then the children were given access to the same doll and other toys.

What happened next was striking. Children who had observed the aggression imitated it, hitting, kicking, and punching the doll. The effect was just as strong when they had watched a filmed model rather than a live one, suggesting that learning could occur through media—a finding with major implications for television and its influence on children.

There were subtle differences. Girls imitated aggression only if the model was female; boys imitated regardless of the model's sex, suggesting that gendered social norms around who should be aggressive were already forming even in such young children. The effect was strongest in the immediate aftermath of observation, but children showed aggression even when the model was no longer present, indicating that the learning had been internalized.

Bandura's conclusion was radical for his time: reinforcement was not necessary for learning to occur. Observation and imitation alone were sufficient. This contradicted Skinner's emphasis on environmental consequences. The work became foundational to social learning theory and sparked decades of research—and public concern—about the effects of media violence on children.
